items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose we want to evaluate the double integral

Content:
[MATH: \displaystyle \iint\limits_{D} 2(x+y)\,\textrm{d}A,]
where [MATH: D] is the finite region bounded by the lines [MATH: x=0, \, y=1, \, y=2, \, y=3-x,] and [MATH: y=x.] How do we proceed?

Content:
To evaluate an integral like this, we carry out the following steps:

Content:
Step 1. Sketch the region [MATH: D]. This allows us to determine the precise set-up of our integral.

Content:
In this example, we obtain the following:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/a64f0d6e7fc9604a146826a9c4d44ce3]

Content:
Step 2. Split (if necessary) the region [MATH: D] into several type I or II regions.

Content:
From the diagram above, we see that our region [MATH: D] can be partitioned into two type I regions [MATH: D_1] and [MATH: D_2,] as follows.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/00452a48ba8d7e85e9bd6854e50e5882]

Content:
So, we get

Content:
[MATH: D_1 = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \quad 1 \leq y \leq 2\big\}]
and
[MATH: D_2= \{(x,y)\: : \: 1 \leq x \leq 3/2, \quad x \leq y \leq 3-x\}]

Content:
Step 3. Set up and evaluate the integral using the additivity property of double integrals. We recall the following fact:

Content:
> If [MATH: D] is the union of two sub-regions, [MATH: D_1, D_2], that don't overlap then,
> [MATH: \iint\limits_{D} f(x,y)\ \textrm d A = \iint\limits_{D_1} f(x,y)\ \textrm d A + \iint\limits_{D_2} f(x,y)\ \textrm d A.]

Content:
So, finally, we obtain

Content:
[MATH: ∬_(D)2(x + y)dA|= ∬_(D_{1})2(x + y)dA + ∬_(D_{2})2(x + y)dA; = ∫_{0}^{1}∫_{1}^{2}2(x + y)dydx + ∫_{1}^{3/2}∫_{x}^{3 − x}2(x + y)dydx.]

sections.normalized_html: The region [MATH: D] is enclosed by the curves [MATH: x=2y^3-2y] and [MATH: x=y^3-4y,] and the [MATH: y]-axis, as shown in the picture. Evaluate the double integral [MATH: \displaystyle \iint\limits_{D} \mathrm{d}A.]
sections.readable_text:
[IMG: /graphics/ad479776abe1b64937bf9c79c413a827]

The region [MATH: D] is enclosed by the curves [MATH: x=2y^3-2y] and [MATH: x=y^3-4y,] and the [MATH: y]-axis, as shown in the picture. Evaluate the double integral [MATH: \displaystyle \iint\limits_{D} \mathrm{d}A.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The region [MATH: D] can be partitioned into two type II regions [MATH: D_1] and [MATH: D_2,] as shown below.

As a result, we get

[MATH: D_1 = \bigg\{ (x,y) \: : \: -2 \leq y \leq 0, \quad 0 \leq x \leq y^3\!-\!4y \bigg\}]

and

[MATH: D_2 = \bigg\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq y \leq 1, \quad 2y^3\!-\!2y \leq x \leq 0 \bigg\}.]

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose we want to evaluate the double integral

Content:
[MATH: \displaystyle \iint\limits_{D} 2(x+y)\,\textrm{d}A,]
where [MATH: D] is the finite region bounded by the lines [MATH: x=0, \, y=1, \, y=2, \, y=3-x,] and [MATH: y=x.] How do we proceed?

Content:
To evaluate an integral like this, we carry out the following steps:

Content:
Step 1. Sketch the region [MATH: D]. This allows us to determine the precise set-up of our integral.

Content:
In this example, we obtain the following:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/a64f0d6e7fc9604a146826a9c4d44ce3]

Content:
Step 2. Split (if necessary) the region [MATH: D] into several type I or II regions.

Content:
From the diagram above, we see that our region [MATH: D] can be partitioned into two type I regions [MATH: D_1] and [MATH: D_2,] as follows.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/00452a48ba8d7e85e9bd6854e50e5882]

Content:
So, we get

Content:
[MATH: D_1 = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \quad 1 \leq y \leq 2\big\}]
and
[MATH: D_2= \{(x,y)\: : \: 1 \leq x \leq 3/2, \quad x \leq y \leq 3-x\}]

Content:
Step 3. Set up and evaluate the integral using the additivity property of double integrals. We recall the following fact:

Content:
> If [MATH: D] is the union of two sub-regions, [MATH: D_1, D_2], that don't overlap then,
> [MATH: \iint\limits_{D} f(x,y)\ \textrm d A = \iint\limits_{D_1} f(x,y)\ \textrm d A + \iint\limits_{D_2} f(x,y)\ \textrm d A.]

Content:
So, finally, we obtain

Content:
[MATH: ∬_(D)2(x + y)dA|= ∬_(D_{1})2(x + y)dA + ∬_(D_{2})2(x + y)dA; = ∫_{0}^{1}∫_{1}^{2}2(x + y)dydx + ∫_{1}^{3/2}∫_{x}^{3 − x}2(x + y)dydx.]

---

Item 2 — Example: Representing a Double Integral as a Repeated Integral Over a Union of Type I Regions

Express the double integral of a function [MATH: f(x,y)] over the region [MATH: D] as a sum of repeated integrals over type I regions.

[IMG: /graphics/44c00a18090dd9acfb716d4de0839aed]

Content:
EXPLANATION

The region [MATH: D] can be partitioned into two type I regions [MATH: D_1] and [MATH: D_2,] as shown below.

[IMG: /graphics/dfed9d77548799c30e813d5415b96807]

As a result, we get

[MATH: D_1 = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \quad \sqrt x \leq y \leq 2^x \big\}]

and

[MATH: D_2 = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 1 \leq x \leq 4, \quad \sqrt x \leq y \leq 2 \big\}.]

Therefore, using the additivity property of double integrals, we obtain
[MATH: ∬_(D)f(x, y)dA|= ∬_(D_{1})f(x, y)dA + ∬_(D_{2})f(x, y)dA; = ∫_{0}^{1}∫_{sqrt(x)}^{2^{x}}f(x, y)dydx + ∫_{1}^{4}∫_{sqrt(x)}^{2}f(x, y)dydx.]
